docs.title: PatternTester
docs.text:
Professional Monitor Test Pattern Generator

PatternTester is an open-source application designed to evaluate, verify and analyze the performance of display devices using professional test patterns.

The project is intended for:

  • Display manufacturers
  • System integrators
  • Service technicians
  • Quality control laboratories
  • AV professionals
  • Enthusiasts and retro-computing users

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Cross-platform (Windows / Linux)
  • Multi-monitor support
  • Native Avalonia UI
  • Real-time pattern rendering
  • High-DPI aware
  • Portable configuration
  • Open Source (GPL v3)

docs.title: Supported Test Categories
docs.text:
• Geometry
  • Grayscale
  • Gamma
  • Sharpness
  • Focus
  • Color
  • Contrast
  • Gradients
  • Uniformity
  • Alignment
  • Pixel Mapping
  • Custom patterns

docs.title: Project Goals
docs.text:
PatternTester has been designed with four main objectives:

  1. Professional monitor testing
  2. Cross-platform compatibility
  3. Clean software architecture
  4. Long-term maintainability

The software is not only a pattern generator but also a technical reference for monitor testing and calibration.

docs.title: Lingue esterne di Pattern Tester
docs.text: Le lingue dell'interfaccia sono caricate dalla cartella Languages accanto all'eseguibile.

docs.title: Aggiungere una lingua
docs.text:
Copiare it.json o en.json in un nuovo file, ad esempio de.json, e tradurre i valori. Il campo _code identifica la lingua e _name è il nome mostrato nelle Impostazioni.

Esempio:

{
  "_code": "de",
  "_name": "Deutsch",
  "_help": "PatternTester_Guida_de.html",
  "Menu.File": "_Datei"
}

Il programma rileva automaticamente i nuovi file .json al successivo avvio. Non è necessario ricompilare.

Se _help non viene indicato oppure il file HTML non esiste, la Guida utilizza automaticamente la versione italiana come fallback.

Le traduzioni mancanti in un file vengono inoltre completate usando it.json.

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text: PatternTester is a desktop application, not a networked service — there is no REST/HTTP API. This page documents the public surface of PatternTester.Core, the platform-independent library that defines what a test pattern is and how it is rendered. It has no dependency on Avalonia or any UI framework, so it can be reused or unit-tested in isolation (see tests/PatternTester.Core.Tests).

docs.title: PatternBase
docs.text:
Abstract base class every pattern derives from.

public abstract class PatternBase
{
    protected PatternBase(string name, string? iconName = null);

    public string Name { get; }
    public string? IconName { get; }

    // If true, the rendering engine draws a red border around each
    // cell after the pattern itself has been rendered.
    public virtual bool DrawCellBorder => false;

    public abstract void Render(IPatternRenderContext context, PatternArea area, int cellNumber);
}

Render is called once per grid cell (see Columns and Rows in the User Guide) with the destination PatternArea and the zero-based cellNumber, so a pattern can vary its output across cells if needed (most patterns render the same content in every cell).

docs.title: PatternCatalog
docs.text:
Holds the ordered list of every built-in pattern, in the same order they appear in the Pattern menu.

public sealed class PatternCatalog
{
    public IReadOnlyList<PatternBase> Items { get; }
    public PatternBase this[int index] { get; }
}

docs.title: Built-in Patterns
docs.text:
All under PatternTester.Core.Patterns, each a concrete PatternBase:

Class Menu name GeometryPattern Geometry SingleColorPattern Single Color GrayPattern Gray GammaPattern Gamma BarsPattern Bars ColorBarsPattern Color Bars GradientToBlackPattern Gradient to Black GradientTwoColorsPattern Two-Color Gradient ChessboardPattern Chessboard PhasePattern Phase ColorTemperaturePattern Color Temperature

See Pattern Reference for what each one is used for from a user's perspective.

docs.title: Adding a New Pattern
docs.text:
1. Create a new class under PatternTester.Core/Patterns/ deriving from PatternBase.
  2. Implement Render(...), using the IPatternRenderContext passed in to draw.
  3. Register it in PatternCatalog's constructor, in the position you want it to appear in the Pattern menu.
  4. Add a Pattern.<Name> string to both Languages/it.json and Languages/en.json in PatternTester.App.
  5. If the pattern has configurable parameters, add the corresponding controls to the settings panel in MainWindow.axaml (bound to a new property on MainWindowViewModel), following the pattern used by the existing ones (e.g. Gamma's numeric value, Chessboard's grid size).

docs.title: PatternTester.Rendering
docs.text: PatternCanvas (in PatternTester.Rendering) is the Avalonia control that hosts a PatternBase and turns its Render calls into actual pixels on screen, handling the column/row grid layout and the optional cell border. It is the one piece of Rendering that does depend on Avalonia — Core itself stays UI-framework-agnostic.

docs.title: Multi-Monitor (Windows)
docs.text:
• Fixed a bug where the pattern was always shown on monitor 1, even after selecting a different monitor from the Display menu (the issue was in the menu's data binding, not in window placement).
  • Added an application manifest with Per-Monitor-V2 DPI awareness, required for correct positioning on Windows systems with multiple monitors using different scaling percentages.
  • Added a native Win32 placement fallback as extra protection against known Avalonia Windows-backend bugs in multi-monitor setups.
  • Fixed a rendering bug affecting scaling percentages other than 100% (e.g. 125%): the pattern could appear clipped at the edges (for example, an incomplete border on the Geometry pattern).

docs.title: Info Monitor Window
docs.text:
• Full data now available on Windows too (resolution, refresh rate, physical size, operating system, etc.) — previously available on Linux only.
  • Fixed duplicated/wrapped rows.
  • The window now stays visible above the fullscreen pattern even with a single monitor, instead of ending up hidden behind it.

docs.title: Identify Monitors Window
docs.text: • Added resolution (and, on Windows, refresh rate) below the monitor number, to make it easier to recognize each screen at a glance in multi-monitor setups.

docs.title: Appearance and Customization
docs.text:
• New application icon (color bars).
  • Selectable light/dark application theme from Settings, with the preference saved across restarts.
  • Settings window reorganized into tabs (Appearance, Startup, Default Values, Saving).
  • Consistent typography across every window of the application.
  • Active monitor/columns/rows are now highlighted in the Display menu, correctly restored on restart.

docs.title: About Window
docs.text:
• Removed duplicated rows (Developed by / License).
  • Fixed alignment of all fields (Developed by, License, Version, Website, GitHub) onto a single column.

docs.title: Distribution
docs.text:
• Added an automated build/packaging script and a Windows installer (Inno Setup), producing a self-contained executable that does not require .NET to be preinstalled on the target machine.
  • Installer shows the GPL-3.0 license before installation and offers optional changelog/known-issues pages at the end, with a fully translated (Italian/English) setup wizard.

docs.title: Developer Guide
docs.text: This guide describes the internal structure of PatternTester and how to work on it.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• .NET SDK — exact version pinned in global.json (rollForward: latestFeature, so any compatible newer feature release also works)
  • Avalonia UI 12.x (via NuGet, restored automatically)
  • Git
  • An editor: Visual Studio Community, VS Code + C# Dev Kit, or JetBrains Rider all work; the project has no editor-specific files
  • On Windows, for the installer only: Inno Setup (free)

PatternTester targets net10.0, plain (not net10.0-windows), so the solution builds and runs on both Windows and Linux from the same codebase.

docs.title: Repository Layout
docs.text:
src/
  PatternTester.App/            Avalonia UI application (entry point)
  PatternTester.Core/           Pattern definitions, models, pattern catalog
  PatternTester.Infrastructure/ Configuration persistence
  PatternTester.Rendering/      Pattern drawing/canvas logic
tests/
  PatternTester.Core.Tests/     Unit tests for PatternTester.Core
installer/                      Inno Setup script + packaging PowerShell script
docs/                           This documentation (MkDocs Material)
assets/                         Repository-level images (icon, README screenshots)

Each project has a single responsibility: Core has no UI or platform dependency, Rendering turns pattern definitions into pixels, Infrastructure only knows how to read/write the JSON settings file, and App wires everything together with Avalonia.

docs.title: PatternTester.App Layout
docs.text:
App.axaml / App.axaml.cs        Application entry point, theme setup
MainWindow.axaml(.cs)           Main control window (menus, pattern config panel)
PatternWindow.axaml(.cs)        Fullscreen pattern display window
SettingsWindow.axaml(.cs)       Tabbed settings dialog
MonitorInfoWindow.axaml(.cs)    Detailed per-monitor information panel
MonitorIdentificationWindow.*   Fullscreen "MONITOR n" overlay used by Identify Monitors
AboutWindow.axaml(.cs)          About dialog
ViewModels/                     MainWindowViewModel and supporting view-model types
Services/                       Platform services (see below)
Styles/Theme.axaml              Shared design tokens (colors, card style, base font size)
Languages/it.json, en.json      UI string tables
Assets/                         Icon (.ico/.png) and built-in pattern preview images

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
Service Purpose LinuxMonitorInfoService Populates Info Monitor fields on Linux by shelling out to xrandr/xdpyinfo WindowsMonitorInfoService Same purpose on Windows, via P/Invoke (EnumDisplaySettings, GetDeviceCaps) — no external process needed Win32WindowPlacement Native SetWindowPos fallback used to position the fullscreen pattern window on Windows, in addition to Avalonia's own Window.Position/Screens APIs LocalizationService Loads Languages/*.json and exposes translated strings as dynamic resources

LinuxMonitorInfoService and WindowsMonitorInfoService are not behind a shared interface; the caller (MainWindow.axaml.cs) branches on OperatingSystem.IsWindows() and calls the appropriate one directly. Each method degrades gracefully (returns "N/D"/"N/A" for a field) rather than throwing, so a missing platform API never crashes the info panel.

docs.title: Theming
docs.text:
Styles/Theme.axaml is merged into App.axaml after <FluentTheme />, so its resources take precedence:

  • SystemAccentColor and its light/dark variants are overridden with the application's own accent color — this alone re-colors every FluentTheme control that uses the accent (buttons, sliders, toggle switches, menu highlights) without needing custom ControlTemplates.
  • Colors that must differ between light and dark mode (card/header backgrounds, muted text) live inside ResourceDictionary.ThemeDictionaries, keyed "Dark" / "Light", and are referenced with DynamicResource so they switch live.
  • A global Style Selector="TextBlock" sets the base font size for the whole app; any window/control with an explicit local FontSize overrides it, since local values always win over style setters in Avalonia.
  • A global Style Selector="Window" sets Background="{DynamicResource AppWindowBackgroundBrush}" on every window, replacing FluentTheme's plain white light-mode background with a softer off-white.

The active theme is controlled by Application.Current.RequestedThemeVariant (ThemeVariant.Light / .Dark), toggled from MainWindowViewModel.UseDarkTheme / UseLightTheme and applied in MainWindow.ApplyTheme().

To add a new shared design token: add it to Theme.axaml (inside ThemeDictionaries if it must differ per theme, or as a plain resource otherwise) and reference it elsewhere with {DynamicResource YourKey} — never hardcode a color for anything that should adapt to the theme.

docs.title: Configuration Persistence
docs.text:
PatternTester.Infrastructure.ConfigurationService reads and writes a single JSON file:

  • Windows: %APPDATA%\PatternTester\patterntester.json
  • Linux: ~/.config/PatternTester/patterntester.json

It hydrates a DisplaySettings object (current pattern, monitor, columns/rows) and an ApplicationSettings object (theme, startup mode, save mode, language, default values) at startup, and serializes them back on save. MainWindowViewModel's constructor calls Load() and then must explicitly re-run the "highlight the active option" logic (UpdateColumnSelection, UpdateRowSelection, and — via RefreshMonitors() — UpdateMonitorSelection) for any menu item that mirrors a loaded value, because the constructor sets backing fields directly rather than through the property setters that normally trigger those updates.

When adding a new persisted setting: add the property to ApplicationSettings (or DisplaySettings), add it to the private SettingsData/equivalent DTO in ConfigurationService, and wire both Load() and Save().

docs.title: Multi-Monitor and DPI Handling
docs.text:
This is the area most worth understanding before touching window-placement code.

  • Avalonia's Screen.Bounds is expressed in physical pixels.
  • Avalonia's Window.Width / Window.Height are expressed in logical pixels (DIPs).
  • At 100% display scaling the two coincide, which can hide bugs during casual testing; at any other scaling (125%, 150%, ...) a window sized directly from Screen.Bounds.Width/Height ends up larger or smaller than the physical screen, clipping content at the edges.

The fix applied throughout PatternWindow and MonitorIdentificationWindow is to always divide by Screen.Scaling when assigning Width/Height:

Width  = screen.Bounds.Width  / screen.Scaling;
Height = screen.Bounds.Height / screen.Scaling;

Window.Position (a PixelPoint) is already in physical pixels and needs no conversion.

On Windows, PatternWindow also re-applies its position/size through Win32WindowPlacement (native SetWindowPos) after Show(), as a defensive measure against a known Avalonia Win32-backend quirk where a window's initial placement can be reset during creation. app.manifest declares Per-Monitor-V2 DPI awareness, which is required for Windows to report correct per-monitor scaling in the first place — without it, Windows applies DPI virtualization and the numbers above are unreliable.

Menu selection binding pitfall: menu items generated from an ItemsSource (e.g. the Monitor/Columns/Rows submenus) with a Click handler attached to the parent MenuItem will report the parent as sender when the click bubbles up, not the clicked child. Handlers for those menus read e.Source instead of sender, or (preferred, used for Columns/Rows/Monitor) attach Click directly to each generated ToggleButton via the DataTemplate, so sender is correct without relying on bubbling at all.

docs.title: Building
docs.text:
dotnet restore
dotnet build
dotnet test
dotnet run --project src/PatternTester.App

docs.title: Publishing a Windows Executable
docs.text: dotnet publish src/PatternTester.App/PatternTester.App.csproj -c Release -r win-x64 --self-contained true -p:PublishSingleFile=true -p:IncludeNativeLibrariesForSelfExtract=true -o publish

docs.title: Building the Windows Installer
docs.text:
installer/build-and-package.ps1 automates the two steps above plus Inno Setup compilation:

.\installer\build-and-package.ps1

Optional parameters: -Version "1.2.0", -SkipInstaller (publish only). It looks for ISCC.exe (Inno Setup's command-line compiler) and offers to install it via winget if missing. The generated installer:

  • copies the self-contained executable, LICENSE.txt, CHANGELOG.txt and KNOWN_ISSUES.txt into the install directory;
  • shows the GPL-3.0 license (LicenseFile=) before installation, translated setup UI (Italian/English via [Languages]);
  • offers optional "View changelog" / "View known issues" checkboxes on the final page.

installer/PatternTester.iss and installer/build-and-package.ps1 both resolve paths relative to their own location, so they work whether installer/ sits at the repository root or is moved (as long as the two files stay together and src/ stays one level above).

docs.title: Coding Guidelines
docs.text:
• Keep methods short and single-purpose.
  • Prefer composition over inheritance.
  • Avoid duplicated logic between the Windows and Linux code paths where the underlying data is the same shape (see WindowsMonitorInfoService/LinuxMonitorInfoService for the accepted exception: platform-specific data sources with a shared consumer).
  • All source code comments must be written in English (Italian is fine in commit messages/PRs/discussions, not in code).
  • Never hardcode a themeable color; use Theme.axaml resources.
  • When adding a window, follow the existing pattern: apply Classes="card" to grouping Borders, Classes="section-title" to section headers, and reference Icon="avares://PatternTester.App/Assets/icon.png" (the .ico is Windows-executable-icon only, not for in-app window icons — Avalonia's own image decoder handles .png more reliably than multi-resolution .ico).

docs.title: Version Control
docs.text:
• Feature branches, small commits, descriptive messages.
  • Pull requests for anything touching shared infrastructure (Theme.axaml, ConfigurationService, ApplicationSettings).
  • Update this documentation when a change affects architecture, persisted settings, or platform-specific behavior.

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text: See installer/KNOWN_ISSUES.txt for the current list (per-channel color depth unavailable on Windows without EDID parsing, refresh-rate lookup depending on Avalonia's reported device name matching Windows' own naming, etc.).

docs.title: Why doesn't the pattern fill the screen?
docs.text:
Ensure:

  • fullscreen mode is enabled
  • monitor scaling is correct
  • native resolution is selected

docs.title: Why are monitors numbered differently?
docs.text:
Operating systems determine monitor order.

Use Identify Monitors to verify numbering.

docs.title: Why is the refresh rate not displayed?
docs.text:
Currently:

  • Windows supports refresh rate detection.
  • Linux implementation is still evolving.

docs.title: Does PatternTester support CRT monitors?
docs.text:
Yes.

CRT displays are fully supported provided the operating system recognizes the display correctly.

docs.title: Does PatternTester support multiple monitors?
docs.text:
Yes.

Multiple monitors are one of the core design goals.

docs.title: Is internet access required?
docs.text:
No.

PatternTester operates completely offline.

docs.title: Is PatternTester open source?
docs.text:
Yes.

PatternTester is released under GPL-3.0.

docs.title: Which platforms are supported?
docs.text:
Currently:

  • Windows

In development:

  • Linux

Future ports remain possible thanks to Avalonia.

docs.title: User Guide
docs.text:
Welcome to the PatternTester User Guide.

This document explains how to install, configure and use PatternTester for professional monitor evaluation.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
PatternTester is a cross-platform (Windows and Linux) monitor test pattern generator, designed to evaluate display characteristics such as geometry, gamma, color accuracy, sharpness and uniformity. It supports multiple monitors simultaneously, each with independent configuration.

Typical use cases:

  • Display calibration and quality control
  • Comparing multiple monitors side by side
  • AV installation testing
  • Enthusiast/professional display evaluation

docs.title: Main Window
docs.text: The main window is the control panel: it lets you choose a pattern, configure its parameters, and choose which monitor to show it on. The actual test pattern is displayed full-screen in a separate window, so the main window stays available to adjust settings while you look at the result.

docs.title: Menu Bar
docs.text: Menu Contains File Save configuration, Settings, Exit Display Monitor selection, number of columns/rows for the split-screen patterns Pattern Choice of test pattern (see Pattern Reference) View Show pattern (fullscreen), Info Monitor, Identify Monitors Help User guide, About

docs.title: Pattern Configuration Panel
docs.text: Below the menu, a panel shows the parameters for the currently selected pattern (for example, gamma value, grid size, number of color bars, gradient direction). Only the fields relevant to the active pattern are shown; the rest stay hidden.

docs.title: Choosing a Monitor
docs.text: Open Display → Monitor to pick which connected screen the pattern will appear on. The monitor currently selected is highlighted. This works the same way whether one or several monitors are connected, and the choice is remembered the next time you launch PatternTester (see Settings).

docs.title: Identifying Monitors
docs.text: If you are not sure which physical screen corresponds to which number in the menu, use View → Identify Monitors. A large label briefly appears on every connected screen, showing its number, resolution and (on Windows) refresh rate — for example MONITOR 2 followed by 1920x1080@60. This is especially useful right after connecting a new monitor or in installations with several identical screens.

docs.title: Info Monitor
docs.text: View → Info Monitor opens a panel with detailed information about the selected screen: resolution, refresh rate, physical size, color depth, scaling, orientation, and information about the operating system session. Available fields differ slightly between Windows and Linux, depending on what each platform exposes.

docs.title: Columns and Rows (Split-Screen Patterns)
docs.text: Some patterns (for example the chessboard) are drawn as a grid. Display → Columns and Display → Rows control how many horizontal and vertical divisions are used. The active values are highlighted in the menu, the same way the active monitor is.

docs.title: Fullscreen Display
docs.text:
View → Show Pattern displays the currently selected pattern fullscreen on the chosen monitor, above every other window. To go back to the controls:

  • Right-click anywhere on the pattern, or
  • Untick View → Show Pattern again from the main window.

The pattern window automatically matches the exact resolution and position of the target monitor, including on systems where different monitors use different Windows display-scaling percentages.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
File → Settings opens a dedicated window, organized in tabs:

Tab Contents Appearance Light or dark application theme Startup Whether to reopen with the last-used configuration or with defaults; whether to show the pattern automatically at startup Default Values Default pattern, monitor, language, columns and rows used when "start with defaults" is selected Saving When to persist the configuration: on exit, on every change, or only when File → Save is used manually

Settings (and, depending on the chosen save mode, the last-used pattern/monitor/layout) are stored in a per-user configuration file:

  • Windows: %APPDATA%\PatternTester\patterntester.json
  • Linux: ~/.config/PatternTester/patterntester.json

docs.title: Language
docs.text: PatternTester ships with Italian and English translations, selectable from Settings → Default Values → Language.

docs.title: Typical Workflow
docs.text:
1. Connect and, if needed, identify your monitor(s) (View → Identify Monitors).
  2. Select the target monitor (Display → Monitor).
  3. Choose a pattern (Pattern menu) and adjust its parameters in the main panel.
  4. Show it fullscreen (View → Show Pattern).
  5. Evaluate the display; right-click to return to the controls.
  6. Repeat for each pattern you want to check, and for each monitor.

docs.title: The pattern looks cut off or larger than the screen
docs.text: This is almost always a Windows display-scaling issue (e.g. 125% or 150% scaling). PatternTester accounts for per-monitor scaling automatically; if you still see this, check Info Monitor for the scaling percentage reported for that screen, and make sure you are running the latest version.

docs.title: The pattern appears on the wrong monitor
docs.text: Use View → Identify Monitors to confirm the physical numbering, then re-select the correct one from Display → Monitor.

docs.title: The "Info Monitor" window is missing information
docs.text: Some fields (in particular per-channel color depth) are not exposed by Windows without parsing the monitor's raw EDID data, which PatternTester does not currently do; these fields show "N/A". On Linux, the same information is normally available through xrandr.

docs.title: After closing "Info Monitor", the main window ends up behind the pattern
docs.text: Make sure you are on the latest release — this was a known issue in earlier builds, fixed by keeping the main window on top while returning from the info panel.

docs.text: This section describes Windows-specific information.

docs.title: Supported Versions
docs.text:
PatternTester supports:

  • Windows 10
  • Windows 11

Both x64 and ARM64 are planned.

docs.text:
• .NET Runtime
  • DirectX compatible graphics driver

docs.title: Monitor Detection
docs.text:
PatternTester retrieves:

  • monitor name
  • native resolution
  • refresh rate

The application automatically detects all connected displays.

docs.title: Monitor Identification
docs.text:
The Identify Monitors function displays a temporary fullscreen window on each monitor.

Displayed information includes:

  • monitor number
  • native resolution
  • refresh rate (Windows)

Example:

Monitor 2

2560 × 1440 @ 144 Hz

docs.title: DPI Awareness
docs.text:
PatternTester is High-DPI aware.

Recommended Windows scaling:

  • 100%
  • 125%
  • 150%

Fullscreen rendering always uses the monitor native resolution.

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text:
Some USB display adapters may report incomplete monitor information.

Refresh rate detection depends on the graphics driver.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Adobe RGB extends the color gamut beyond sRGB, especially in green and cyan regions.

It is widely used in professional photography and printing.

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• Photography
  • Graphic design
  • Print production
  • Prepress

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
Verify:

  • wide gamut coverage
  • smooth gradients
  • neutral grayscale

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The Aspect Ratio pattern verifies that the displayed image maintains the correct geometric proportions.

Incorrect aspect ratio causes circles to appear as ellipses and squares as rectangles.

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• Monitor setup
  • Television calibration
  • HDMI devices
  • Media players
  • Retro computers
  • Game consoles

docs.title: Expected Result
docs.text:
The display should preserve:

  • perfect circles
  • square grids
  • equal horizontal and vertical scaling

docs.title: Horizontal Stretch
docs.text:
Objects appear wider than expected.

Possible causes:

  • incorrect monitor settings
  • GPU scaling
  • television overscan

docs.title: Vertical Stretch
docs.text: Objects appear taller than expected.

docs.title: Non-Uniform Scaling
docs.text: Different scaling factors are applied horizontally and vertically.

docs.title: Professional Notes
docs.text: Aspect Ratio verification should always precede geometry testing.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• VESA
  • HDMI

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Backlight Bleeding patterns reveal unwanted light leakage from the LCD backlight.

This phenomenon does not affect OLED displays.

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• LCD inspection
  • Manufacturing quality control
  • Customer acceptance testing

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
Display a completely black fullscreen pattern.

Inspect:

  • corners
  • edges
  • center

docs.title: Expected Result
docs.text: The screen should appear uniformly black.

docs.title: Corner Bleeding
docs.text: Light leakage near corners.

docs.title: Edge Bleeding
docs.text: Bright regions appear along display borders.

docs.title: Pressure Spots
docs.text: Localized bright areas caused by panel stress.

docs.title: Professional Notes
docs.text:
Backlight bleeding should always be evaluated:

  • in a dark room
  • after monitor warm-up
  • at normal brightness settings

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• ISO 9241
  • VESA

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The Black Level pattern determines whether the display correctly reproduces the darkest visible luminance levels.

Correct black level adjustment is essential before evaluating gamma, contrast and grayscale.

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• Monitor calibration
  • Television setup
  • OLED evaluation
  • LCD evaluation
  • Projector adjustment

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
A properly adjusted monitor should display:

  • reference black
  • first visible gray steps
  • uniform dark background

Very dark levels should remain distinguishable.

docs.title: Black Crush
docs.text:
Shadow details disappear.

Typical causes:

  • excessive contrast
  • incorrect gamma
  • dynamic contrast
  • HDR configuration

docs.title: Raised Blacks
docs.text:
The image appears washed out.

Black areas become gray.

docs.title: Professional Notes
docs.text:
Perform the test in a dark room.

Disable:

  • Dynamic Contrast
  • Black Equalizer
  • Adaptive Brightness

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• ITU-R BT.709
  • VESA

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Black Uniformity evaluates how consistently the display reproduces black across the entire panel.

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• LCD quality control
  • OLED inspection
  • HDR verification

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
Display a full black screen.

Inspect:

  • center
  • corners
  • edges

docs.title: Expected Result
docs.text: The screen should appear uniformly dark.

docs.title: Clouding
docs.text: Random brighter regions become visible.

docs.title: Backlight Leakage
docs.text: Light escapes from panel edges.

docs.title: Panel Glow
docs.text: Brightness changes depending on viewing angle.

docs.title: Professional Notes
docs.text:
Allow the monitor to warm up before testing.

Ambient lighting should be minimized.

docs.title: References
docs.text: • ISO 9241

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The Blooming pattern evaluates the halo effect generated by local dimming systems around bright objects displayed on dark backgrounds.

Blooming is mainly observed on:

  • Full Array Local Dimming LCD
  • MiniLED displays

OLED displays normally do not exhibit blooming.

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• HDR verification
  • Local dimming evaluation
  • Display comparison

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
Display one or more bright objects over a black background.

Observe:

  • halo size
  • halo intensity
  • symmetry
  • movement

docs.title: Expected Result
docs.text: Bright objects should remain isolated without illuminating adjacent dark areas.

docs.title: Large Halo
docs.text: The illuminated area extends well beyond the bright object.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The checkerboard pattern evaluates contrast, local dimming and pixel response.

It is particularly useful for LCD, MiniLED and OLED displays.

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• Contrast verification
  • Local dimming evaluation
  • Blooming detection
  • Uniformity inspection

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
Observe:

  • edge sharpness
  • blooming
  • luminance consistency
  • black level

docs.title: Blooming
docs.text: Bright squares illuminate surrounding dark areas.

docs.title: Halo
docs.text: Bright edges become visible around white regions.

docs.title: Poor Contrast
docs.text: Black areas appear gray.

docs.title: Professional Notes
docs.text: Perform this test in a dark environment for best results.

docs.title: Related Standards
docs.text: • VESA DisplayHDR

docs.title: References
docs.text: • VESA

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Chroma Resolution evaluates the display's ability to reproduce fine color detail independently from luminance detail.

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• Video processor evaluation
  • Broadcast equipment
  • HDMI verification
  • Compression testing

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
Inspect colored fine lines and alternating color structures.

Color transitions should remain sharp.

docs.title: Expected Result
docs.text: The monitor should reproduce thin colored details without smearing.

docs.title: Chroma Blur
docs.text: Fine color detail becomes soft.

docs.title: Color Bleeding
docs.text: Adjacent colors merge together.

docs.title: Incorrect Chroma Upsampling
docs.text: Compression artifacts become visible.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Color Bars verify color reproduction accuracy.

This pattern is commonly used in broadcast and video production.

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• Display verification
  • Capture device testing
  • Video pipeline validation
  • Broadcast equipment

docs.title: Expected Result
docs.text:
Each color should appear:

  • saturated
  • uniform
  • clearly separated

No color should bleed into adjacent bars.

docs.title: Common Problems
docs.text:
• incorrect white balance
  • color clipping
  • compression artifacts
  • chroma subsampling

docs.title: Professional Notes
docs.text: Color Bars should be evaluated after grayscale and gamma calibration.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Color Temperature patterns evaluate the display white point.

The white point defines the chromatic appearance of neutral colors.

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• Display calibration
  • Factory quality control
  • Color critical applications
  • Photography
  • Video production

docs.title: Typical White Points
docs.text: Temperature Typical Use 5000 K Printing 6500 K Standard monitor 9300 K Consumer televisions

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
Neutral gray should remain free of:

  • blue tint
  • red tint
  • green tint

docs.title: Blue White
docs.text: Typical of factory monitor presets.

docs.title: Warm White
docs.text: Visible yellow or red cast.

docs.title: Green Tint
docs.text: Usually indicates poor calibration.

docs.title: Professional Notes
docs.text: The industry standard white point for most computer monitors is D65 (6500 K).

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• CIE
  • ISO 12646
  • IEC 61966

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Color Uniformity evaluates whether neutral colors remain consistent across the entire display surface.

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• Professional monitor evaluation
  • Graphic design
  • Photography
  • Print proofing

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
Inspect the display using neutral gray.

The entire screen should exhibit:

  • identical hue
  • identical saturation
  • identical brightness

docs.title: Corner Tint
docs.text: Corners exhibit different colors.

docs.title: Edge Shift
docs.text: Color changes near display borders.

docs.title: Center Drift
docs.text: The center differs from the outer regions.

docs.title: Professional Notes
docs.text: Uniformity becomes easier to evaluate in a controlled lighting environment.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• ISO 12646
  • EIZO Technical Library

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The Contrast pattern evaluates the display's ability to reproduce the difference between the darkest and brightest luminance levels.

Correct contrast adjustment maximizes image quality without losing shadow or highlight detail.

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• Monitor calibration
  • Television setup
  • HDR evaluation
  • Projector adjustment

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
A correctly adjusted display should provide:

  • deep blacks
  • bright whites
  • preserved highlight detail
  • preserved shadow detail

docs.title: Excessive Contrast
docs.text:
Symptoms:

  • white clipping
  • blooming
  • loss of highlight detail

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The Convergence pattern verifies that the red, green and blue image components are perfectly aligned.

Although primarily associated with CRT displays, convergence verification remains useful for projectors and certain image processing systems.

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• CRT adjustment
  • Projector alignment
  • Optical evaluation
  • Image processor verification

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
Observe thin white lines.

Correct convergence produces:

  • perfectly white lines
  • no colored borders
  • uniform alignment across the screen

docs.title: Red Shift
docs.text: A red fringe appears beside white lines.

docs.title: Blue Shift
docs.text: Blue edges become visible.

docs.title: Green Misalignment
docs.text: White lines appear tinted.

docs.title: Professional Notes
docs.text: Evaluate convergence in the screen center first, then near all four corners.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• SMPTE
  • EIA

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Cross Color patterns reveal unwanted interactions between luminance and chrominance.

They are primarily useful for composite video systems and legacy analog equipment.

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• Composite video testing
  • Broadcast equipment
  • Legacy video processors
  • Retro gaming hardware

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
The image should remain:

  • stable
  • free of false colors
  • free of shimmering
  • free of moving artifacts

docs.title: False Color
docs.text: Fine luminance details produce unwanted colors.

docs.title: Dot Crawl
docs.text: Moving color artifacts appear along high-contrast edges.

docs.title: Chroma Interference
docs.text: Color information leaks into luminance detail.

docs.title: Professional Notes
docs.text:
Cross Color evaluation is mainly applicable to composite video sources.

Digital HDMI connections normally do not exhibit these artifacts.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• SMPTE
  • NTSC Engineering Handbook

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Crosshatch patterns verify geometric accuracy and image linearity.

Historically they have been widely used for CRT alignment but remain useful for digital displays.

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• Geometry
  • Convergence
  • Aspect ratio
  • Scaling verification

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
Lines should remain:

  • straight
  • evenly spaced
  • perpendicular

The grid should remain centered across the entire screen.

docs.title: Barrel Distortion
docs.text: Lines curve outward.

docs.title: Pincushion Distortion
docs.text: Lines curve inward.

docs.title: Trapezoid Distortion
docs.text: Vertical edges are no longer parallel.

docs.title: Professional Notes
docs.text: Crosshatch evaluation should always be performed using the monitor native resolution.

docs.title: Related Standards
docs.text:
• SMPTE
  • VESA

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• SMPTE
  • VESA

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
DCI-P3 is a wide color gamut developed for digital cinema.

Today it is commonly used by:

  • OLED monitors
  • HDR televisions
  • Professional video editing
  • Modern smartphones

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• HDR mastering
  • Cinema production
  • Video editing
  • Color grading

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
Inspect:

  • saturated reds
  • greens
  • yellows
  • skin tones

docs.title: Expected Result
docs.text: Colors should remain saturated while preserving smooth gradients.

docs.title: Gamut Compression
docs.text: Wide colors become clipped.

docs.title: Incorrect Mapping
docs.text: The monitor converts colors incorrectly.

docs.title: Excessive Saturation
docs.text: Consumer modes exaggerate color intensity.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Dead Pixel patterns help identify defective LCD, OLED and LED pixels.

The test displays uniform colors covering the entire screen.

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• Incoming inspection
  • Warranty verification
  • Manufacturing QA
  • Monitor acceptance testing

docs.title: Test Colors
docs.text:
Typical inspection colors:

  • Black
  • White
  • Red
  • Green
  • Blue

Each color reveals different pixel defects.

docs.title: Dead Pixel
docs.text: Always black.

docs.title: Stuck Pixel
docs.text: Remains permanently on one color.

docs.title: Hot Pixel
docs.text: Always bright.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Dot Pitch patterns verify the display's capability to reproduce single-pixel structures.

They are useful for evaluating:

  • pixel definition
  • scaling accuracy
  • panel resolution
  • subpixel rendering

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• Native resolution verification
  • Pixel structure inspection
  • Display comparison

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
Inspect the pattern closely.

Individual dots should remain:

  • clearly separated
  • evenly spaced
  • perfectly aligned

docs.title: Blurred Pixels
docs.text: Usually caused by scaling.

docs.title: Missing Pixels
docs.text: May indicate defective pixels or interpolation.

docs.title: Uneven Spacing
docs.text: Can reveal geometry or scaling problems.

docs.title: Professional Notes
docs.text:
Dot Pitch patterns should always be evaluated using the monitor's native resolution.

Disable image sharpening and scaling whenever possible.

docs.title: References
docs.text: • VESA

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The Focus pattern evaluates the ability of a display to reproduce the finest visible details.

It is particularly useful for:

  • LCD monitors
  • CRT displays
  • Projectors
  • Video processors
  • Scaling devices

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• Focus adjustment
  • Optical evaluation
  • Scaling verification
  • Signal path validation

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
Inspect the pattern from the normal viewing distance.

Look for:

  • perfectly sharp intersections
  • clean vertical lines
  • clean horizontal lines
  • no smearing

docs.title: Soft Image
docs.text:
Possible causes:

  • incorrect focus
  • monitor scaling

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The Gamma pattern verifies the luminance response of the display.

Gamma defines the relationship between the digital input value and the light emitted by the monitor.

Incorrect gamma affects contrast perception, shadow detail and highlight rendering.

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• Monitor calibration
  • Quality control
  • Factory verification
  • Color critical work

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
A correct gamma should provide:

  • smooth luminance transitions
  • balanced midtones
  • visible shadow detail
  • preserved highlights

docs.title: Gamma Too Low
docs.text:
Symptoms:

  • washed out image
  • low contrast
  • gray blacks

docs.title: Gamma Too High
docs.text:
Symptoms:

  • crushed shadows
  • excessive contrast
  • loss of dark details

docs.title: Professional Notes
docs.text:
Typical desktop gamma:

  • Windows: 2.2
  • Linux: 2.2
  • macOS: 2.2

Professional workflows may require different target values.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: The geometry grid verifies that the monitor reproduces straight lines with correct proportions.

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• Aspect ratio verification
  • Overscan detection
  • Image centering
  • Pixel mapping
  • Display scaling

docs.title: Expected Result
docs.text:
The grid should appear:

  • perfectly rectangular
  • centered
  • evenly spaced
  • undistorted

docs.title: Overscan
docs.text: Outer lines disappear.

docs.title: Stretching
docs.text: Squares become rectangles.

docs.title: Scaling Errors
docs.text: Lines appear uneven or blurry.

docs.title: Professional Notes
docs.text: Geometry should always be verified using the monitor native resolution.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Detects trailing images caused by slow pixel response.

docs.title: Common Problems
docs.text:
• Smearing
  • Overshoot

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Gradient patterns verify the display's ability to reproduce smooth tonal transitions.

They are used to identify color quantization, banding and processing artifacts.

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• Color depth evaluation
  • HDR verification
  • GPU testing
  • Image processing validation

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
A correct display should show:

  • continuous transitions
  • no visible steps
  • no sudden luminance changes
  • uniform gradients

docs.title: Banding
docs.text:
Visible steps replace smooth transitions.

Typical causes:

  • 6-bit panels
  • incorrect gamma
  • compression
  • poor image processing

docs.title: Posterization
docs.text:
Large regions merge into a single tone.

Usually caused by excessive processing.

docs.title: Professional Notes
docs.text: Gradient evaluation should be performed using native color depth with image enhancements disabled.

docs.title: Related Standards
docs.text:
• VESA DisplayHDR
  • IEC 61966

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• VESA
  • IEC

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: The grayscale pattern evaluates the monitor's ability to reproduce different luminance levels without clipping, crushing or banding.

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• Brightness adjustment
  • Contrast adjustment
  • Gamma verification
  • Black level evaluation
  • White level evaluation

docs.title: What to Look For
docs.text:
A correctly calibrated display should show:

  • distinguishable dark shades
  • distinguishable bright shades
  • smooth transitions
  • no visible banding

docs.title: Black Crush
docs.text:
Dark gray levels become completely black.

Possible causes:

  • excessive contrast
  • incorrect gamma
  • monitor calibration

docs.title: White Clipping
docs.text:
Bright levels merge into pure white.

Possible causes:

  • excessive brightness
  • HDR configuration
  • graphics driver settings

docs.title: Banding
docs.text:
Visible steps instead of smooth gradients.

Possible causes:

  • low color depth
  • incorrect gamma
  • panel limitations

docs.title: Professional Notes
docs.text:
Always evaluate grayscale after the monitor has reached operating temperature.

Ambient light should remain constant throughout the evaluation.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Grid Alignment patterns verify that image elements remain correctly aligned over the entire display area.

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• Flat panel evaluation
  • Projector installation
  • Display wall setup
  • Video processor verification

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
Inspect:

  • line spacing
  • corner alignment
  • edge consistency
  • grid symmetry

docs.title: Curved Lines
docs.text: Usually indicate geometry distortion.

docs.title: Uneven Spacing
docs.text: May reveal scaling artifacts.

docs.title: Edge Compression
docs.text: Grid spacing changes near screen borders.

docs.title: Professional Notes
docs.text: Evaluate the grid from multiple viewing positions to detect perspective errors.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• SMPTE
  • VESA

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
HDR patterns verify the monitor's ability to reproduce images with a much wider dynamic range than Standard Dynamic Range (SDR).

HDR testing evaluates:

  • peak brightness
  • shadow detail
  • tone mapping
  • clipping
  • color volume

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• HDR monitor evaluation
  • Television calibration
  • Professional video production
  • HDR10 verification

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
A properly functioning HDR display should show:

  • bright highlights
  • preserved shadow details
  • smooth transitions
  • natural colors

docs.title: Tone Clipping
docs.text: Very bright details disappear.

docs.title: Raised Black Levels
docs.text: Dark scenes appear gray.

docs.title: Incorrect Tone Mapping
docs.text: Brightness changes abruptly across the image.

docs.title: Color Compression
docs.text: Highly saturated colors lose intensity.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Local Dimming patterns evaluate the performance of displays equipped with independently controlled backlight zones.

This includes:

  • MiniLED
  • Full Array Local Dimming (FALD)
  • Advanced LCD televisions

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• Contrast evaluation
  • HDR verification
  • Blooming analysis

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
Observe:

  • dark backgrounds
  • isolated bright objects
  • moving bright objects

docs.title: Expected Result
docs.text: Bright objects should remain bright without illuminating surrounding dark regions.

docs.title: Blooming
docs.text: Bright objects produce visible halos.

docs.title: Zone Lag
docs.text: Backlight reacts too slowly.

docs.title: Pumping
docs.text: Brightness changes unexpectedly during motion.

docs.title: Professional Notes
docs.text: Perform the evaluation in a completely dark environment.

docs.title: References
docs.text: • VESA DisplayHDR

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The Moiré pattern detects interference generated by repetitive structures.

This test is useful for displays, cameras and image acquisition systems.

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• Camera testing
  • Projector evaluation
  • Monitor scaling
  • Capture card verification

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
The displayed pattern should remain stable.

No moving waves or interference should appear.

docs.title: Moving Bands
docs.text: Usually indicate aliasing.

docs.title: Ripple Patterns
docs.text: Produced by scaling or resampling.

docs.title: False Colors
docs.text: Can appear when chroma processing introduces artifacts.

docs.title: Professional Notes
docs.text:
Moiré patterns are extremely sensitive to scaling algorithms.

Even small changes in image processing may become visible.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Evaluates detail while objects move.

docs.title: Common Problems
docs.text:
• Blur
  • Interpolation artifacts

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The Overscan pattern determines whether the display crops the outer image area.

Overscan was common in CRT televisions but is generally undesirable on modern digital displays.

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• Television setup
  • HDMI verification
  • Media player testing
  • Console calibration

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
All outer borders should remain completely visible.

Corner markers must appear without clipping.

docs.title: Cropped Borders
docs.text: Part of the image disappears outside the visible area.

docs.title: Incorrect Scaling
docs.text: The image fills the screen by enlarging beyond its native dimensions.

docs.title: Professional Notes
docs.text: Modern monitors should normally operate with 1:1 pixel mapping and no overscan.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• HDMI
  • VESA

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Pixel Mapping verifies that one image pixel corresponds exactly to one physical display pixel.

This test is essential for modern LCD and OLED displays.

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• Native resolution verification
  • Scaling detection
  • GPU configuration
  • Monitor setup

docs.title: Expected Result
docs.text:
A correct display should show:

  • perfectly sharp pixels
  • no interpolation
  • no blurred edges
  • no scaling artifacts

docs.title: Interpolation
docs.text:
The image appears soft.

Usually caused by:

  • non-native resolution
  • monitor scaling
  • GPU scaling

docs.title: Overscan
docs.text:
Outer pixels disappear.

Typical on televisions.

docs.title: Incorrect Aspect Ratio
docs.text: Pixels become rectangular instead of square.

docs.title: Professional Notes
docs.text: Always test Pixel Mapping using the monitor native resolution.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Rec.2020 defines the Ultra High Definition television color space.

It supports significantly wider color reproduction than Rec.709.

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• UHD production
  • HDR mastering
  • 4K
  • 8K

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
Inspect:

  • highly saturated colors
  • gradient smoothness
  • clipping
  • tone mapping

docs.title: Expected Result
docs.text: Wide gamut colors should remain distinguishable throughout the visible range.

docs.title: Gamut Compression
docs.text: Wide colors become clipped.

docs.title: Tone Mapping Errors
docs.text: HDR conversion produces inaccurate colors.

docs.title: Color Volume Reduction
docs.text: Bright saturated colors lose intensity.

docs.title: Professional Notes
docs.text: Few displays currently reproduce the complete Rec.2020 color space.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Rec.709 defines the standard color space for High Definition television (HDTV).

It specifies:

  • primary colors
  • white point
  • transfer characteristics
  • matrix coefficients

Rec.709 remains the reference for most SDR video production.

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• HDTV production
  • SDR mastering
  • Broadcast
  • Blu-ray authoring

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
Verify:

  • primary colors
  • grayscale neutrality
  • gamma response
  • color accuracy

docs.title: Expected Result
docs.text: The monitor should reproduce the Rec.709 gamut without clipping or visible hue shifts.

docs.title: Incorrect Gamma
docs.text: Midtones appear too dark or too bright.

docs.title: White Point Shift
docs.text: Neutral gray becomes tinted.

docs.title: Color Errors
docs.text: Primary colors deviate from reference values.

docs.title: Professional Notes
docs.text:
Most professional SDR workflows target:

  • Rec.709
  • Gamma 2.4
  • D65 White Point

docs.title: Related Standards
docs.text: • ITU-R BT.709

docs.title: References
docs.text: • ITU

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Measures pixel transition speed.

docs.title: Common Problems
docs.text:
• Ghosting
  • Motion blur

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Sharpness patterns evaluate the ability of the display to reproduce fine details.

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• focus adjustment
  • monitor sharpness setting
  • scaling verification
  • image processing evaluation

docs.title: Expected Result
docs.text:
The image should appear:

  • crisp
  • stable
  • free of halos
  • without artificial enhancement

docs.title: Excessive Sharpness
docs.text:
Typical symptoms:

  • white halos
  • black halos
  • ringing

docs.title: Low Sharpness
docs.text:
Typical symptoms:

  • blurred edges
  • reduced detail
  • loss of texture

docs.title: Professional Notes
docs.text: Most monitors should be evaluated with image enhancement disabled.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The Siemens Star pattern evaluates image sharpness and optical resolution.

It consists of radial black and white sectors converging toward a common center.

This pattern is widely used in:

  • monitor evaluation
  • projector testing
  • camera lens testing
  • optical systems

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• Focus adjustment
  • Resolution analysis
  • Lens evaluation
  • Scaling verification

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
Observe the center of the star.

A correctly reproduced image should show:

  • clean radial lines
  • symmetric convergence
  • minimal aliasing
  • no false colors

docs.title: Loss of Resolution
docs.text: The center becomes a solid gray circle.

docs.title: Aliasing
docs.text: Jagged radial edges indicate insufficient sampling.

docs.title: Chromatic Aberration
docs.text: Colored fringes appear around high-contrast transitions.

docs.title: Professional Notes
docs.text:
Evaluate the pattern both at normal viewing distance and close inspection.

Scaling and image enhancement may significantly affect the result.

docs.title: Related Standards
docs.text: • ISO 12233

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• ISO
  • Imaging Science Foundation (ISF)

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The sRGB pattern verifies the monitor's ability to reproduce the Standard RGB color space.

sRGB is the default color space used by:

  • Windows
  • Internet
  • Office applications
  • Most consumer software

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• Web graphics
  • General photography
  • Office applications
  • Consumer displays

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
Verify:

  • primary colors
  • neutral gray
  • saturation
  • color transitions

docs.title: Expected Result
docs.text: The display should accurately reproduce the entire sRGB gamut without clipping.

docs.title: Oversaturation
docs.text: Colors appear excessively vivid.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Uniformity patterns reveal brightness and color variations across the display surface.

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• Panel inspection
  • Manufacturing QA
  • Display aging analysis

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
Inspect:

  • center
  • edges
  • corners

The display should appear visually uniform.

docs.title: Clouding
docs.text: Localized brighter areas.

docs.title: Backlight Bleeding
docs.text: Light leakage near the panel edges.

docs.title: Dirty Screen Effect
docs.text: Uneven luminance causing visible patches.

docs.title: Tinting
docs.text: Color shifts across different panel regions.

docs.title: Professional Notes
docs.text:
Uniformity evaluation should be performed in a dark room.

Allow the monitor to warm up before testing.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Viewing Angle patterns evaluate image stability when the observer changes position.

This test is particularly important for LCD technologies.

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• Panel comparison
  • Display quality evaluation
  • Installation verification

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
Observe the display from:

  • front
  • left
  • right
  • above
  • below

Evaluate:

  • brightness
  • contrast
  • color shift

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: The White Level pattern verifies that the display reproduces highlight information without clipping.

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• Contrast adjustment
  • HDR evaluation
  • Video calibration

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
The brightest white should remain distinguishable from the adjacent lighter gray levels.

No highlight detail should disappear.

docs.title: White Clipping
docs.text: Several bright levels merge into pure white.

docs.title: Blooming
docs.text: Bright areas illuminate surrounding pixels.

docs.title: Tone Compression
docs.text: Highlights lose detail.

docs.title: Professional Notes
docs.text: White Level should always be adjusted after Black Level.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• VESA DisplayHDR
  • ITU-R BT.709

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: White Uniformity evaluates the consistency of brightness and color across a white screen.

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• Professional monitor evaluation
  • Print proofing
  • Photography
  • Color grading

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
Display a full white image.

Inspect:

  • brightness
  • tint
  • luminance distribution

docs.title: Expected Result
docs.text:
The display should appear:

  • evenly illuminated
  • neutral
  • free of visible patches

docs.title: Corner Darkening
docs.text: Corners appear darker than the center.

docs.title: Color Tint
docs.text:
Some regions become:

  • warmer
  • cooler
  • green
  • magenta

docs.title: Bright Spots
docs.text: Localized brighter areas become visible.

docs.title: Professional Notes
docs.text: Professional graphics monitors usually specify uniformity compensation.

docs.title: Related Standards
docs.text: • ISO 12646

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• ISO
  • EIZO Technical Library

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The Zone Plate pattern evaluates frequency response, scaling algorithms and aliasing.

It contains concentric sinusoidal structures with continuously increasing spatial frequency.

docs.title: Typical Uses
docs.text:
• Image processing evaluation
  • Scaling verification
  • Camera testing
  • Video processor validation

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
A correct system should display:

  • smooth concentric rings
  • stable image
  • no false structures

docs.title: Aliasing
docs.text: False patterns appear at high spatial frequencies.

docs.title: Ringing
docs.text: Artificial oscillations appear around transitions.

docs.title: Moiré
docs.text: Interference patterns become visible.

docs.title: Professional Notes
docs.text:
Zone Plate patterns are extremely sensitive to resampling algorithms.

They are commonly used to evaluate image processing pipelines.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• SMPTE
  • ISO 12233

docs.title: First Start
docs.text:
When PatternTester starts, the Main Window is displayed.

The interface consists of:

  • Menu Bar
  • Toolbar
  • Pattern Categories
  • Pattern List
  • Status Bar

docs.title: Selecting a Monitor
docs.text: If multiple displays are connected, choose the desired monitor before starting a fullscreen test.

docs.title: Displaying a Pattern
docs.text:
1. Select a category.
  2. Select a pattern.
  3. Double-click the pattern or press Enter.

The selected pattern is displayed fullscreen.

docs.title: Leaving Fullscreen
docs.text:
Press:

  • Esc

or

  • Double-click the screen

depending on the selected configuration.

docs.title: Keyboard Navigation
docs.text:
Arrow keys navigate between patterns.

Enter opens the selected pattern.

Esc closes the current fullscreen pattern.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
Before evaluating a display:

  • Allow the monitor to warm up.
  • Disable automatic brightness.
  • Use the native resolution.
  • Reset image enhancements if required.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
Download the latest release from GitHub.

Run the installer and follow the setup wizard.

After installation PatternTester is available from:

  • Start Menu
  • Desktop shortcut (optional)

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
Extract the application package.

Make the executable executable if necessary:

chmod +x PatternTester

Launch the application.

docs.title: Portable Version
docs.text:
The portable version requires no installation.

Simply extract the archive and execute the application.

docs.title: Updating
docs.text:
Replace the application files with the newer version.

User settings are preserved automatically.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
Use:

Settings

→ Apps

→ PatternTester

→ Uninstall

docs.title: Linux
docs.text: Delete the application directory.

docs.title: Welcome
docs.text:
PatternTester is a professional monitor test pattern generator designed for display evaluation, calibration and verification.

It can be used with:

  • LCD monitors
  • OLED monitors
  • MiniLED displays
  • CRT monitors
  • Televisions
  • Projectors
  • Video processors
  • Capture devices

The application generates high-quality fullscreen test patterns that help evaluate image quality, geometry, color reproduction and display performance.

docs.title: Main Features
docs.text:
• Fullscreen pattern generator
  • Multi-monitor support
  • Native resolution output
  • Pattern categories
  • Favorites
  • Playlists
  • Keyboard shortcuts
  • Multilanguage interface

docs.title: Intended Audience
docs.text:
PatternTester is suitable for:

  • Home users
  • Enthusiasts
  • Photographers
  • Video editors
  • Display reviewers
  • Service technicians
  • Quality assurance laboratories

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Windows or Linux
  • GPU supporting the monitor native resolution
  • .NET Runtime (if required by the selected package)
